site_article.headline: Apple's $1,000 tabletop robot may slip to 2028 as software lags, report says

paragraphs.text: Apple is developing a tabletop home robot that could cost around $1,000, and its launch may slip to 2028, according to a November 2, 2026 report by The Information. The device, code-named J595, places a 9-inch display on a swiveling robotic arm. The Next Web and Android Headlines both summarized the report, and Apple has not announced the product.

Former Apple employees expect the robot to be sold as HomeView Ultra, The Next Web reported, citing The Information. The name would tie it to the $299 HomeView smart home hub that Apple introduced in October 2026, which reaches customers on November 13. Android Headlines noted that the price could end up higher than $1,000 because of rising component costs and recent memory shortages.

According to the report, the device uses cameras and sensors to track its surroundings and act on its own. The arm turns the screen to follow people during FaceTime calls. Ideas discussed for the product included switching on the lights when someone enters a room and telling a cat to get off a table. Android Headlines added that the design draws inspiration from the Pixar lamp and the iMac G4, and that Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has said the screen can rotate 360 degrees.

The hardware was finished about two years ago, The Information reported, and software is now the main obstacle. The software team pushed to delay the launch and to cut the feature list back to a few functions centered on FaceTime and basic home tasks such as turning on lights. Apple is aiming for a 2027 release, but the robot may not ship until 2028.

The report also described thin robotics expertise inside the company. One source said Apple has only about 10 people it would call true roboticists, and many of the engineers who started the project have left. About 300 people work on the robot's software, according to The Next Web's summary.

Former chief executive Tim Cook approved continuing the project. John Ternus, who became CEO on September 1, backs it, along with a separate effort on household robots such as machines that fold clothes, The Next Web reported. Android Headlines said Apple has also experimented with wheeled robots and indoor security drones, though those are far from release. Ternus told WIRED in late October that Apple will not ship "AI for AI's sake."

The report suggests that Apple's robot is limited less by motors and screens than by the software that decides what the device should do on its own. Scaling the features back to FaceTime and simple home automation would make the first version closer to a moving smart display than a general home helper. That cautious approach matches the new CEO's public message, but it also means the most ambitious ideas may wait for a later model.
The next marker is whether Apple confirms the HomeView Ultra name or a 2027 date, since the company has so far said nothing publicly about a robot.
